text:
Cabbage.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn / Winter

Cabbages can feed you for much of the year if you match varieties to their seasons. Spring types give tender greens and small heads; summer and autumn types provide fresh heads for salads, slaws and cooking. Winter, savoy and red cabbages can stand or store into colder months. Types differ in shape, texture, colour, hardiness and speed of hearting.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jan – Dec

Germination

7–12 days

Sowing depth

1/2 in. modules; 3/4 in. seedbed

Row spacing

6 in. between seed rows

Yield per plant

3/4-3 lb

Ready in

Chinese ~10 weeks; other types 20–35 weeks from sowing

Sow

Spring heads Aug–Sep. Summer and winter heads in spring. Quick summer heads under glass Feb–Mar.

Plant spacing

Plants/rows: 12–18 in.; spring greens: 4 in., thin to 12 in.; Chinese: 12 in., rows 18 in.

Transplant

Quick summer heads Apr. Winter crops by midsummer. Spring cabbage in autumn.

Recommended varieties
SUMMER CABBAGES
Greyhound

Traditional pointed summer cabbage; open-pollinated.

SUMMER CABBAGES
Hispi

Fast pointed heads for tender summer crops in small spaces.

SPRING CABBAGES
Duncan F1

A versatile pointed cabbage for spring greens or hearted heads.

WINTER CABBAGES
Tundra

Hardy, firm-headed winter cabbage for fresh supplies in colder months.

RED CABBAGES
Red Drumhead

Traditional red heads for slaws, cooking and pickling.

SAVOY CABBAGES
Vertus

A late savoy with dense heads and crinkled leaves for winter harvests.

Key risks
Club root (finger and toe)

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather.

Cabbage caterpillars

Caterpillars of cabbage white butterfly, cabbage moth and related pests chew holes in leaves and may burrow into cabbage hearts.

Cabbage root fly

Cabbage root fly larvae tunnel into roots and stem bases.

Pigeons

Pigeons strip soft leaf tissue from cabbage and other brassicas, often leaving stalks and veins.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
32
BRASSICAS

Firm the bed before planting.

Tread it firm, rake lightly and clear surface rubbish.

Remove yellow lower leaves.

Do not let them rot against winter cabbage or savoy heads.

Use fertile, well-consolidated soil.

Add organic matter and lime acid ground only if needed.

Soil & preparation
Prepare a sunny bed in autumn; compost or well-rotted manure improves poor soil. Let it settle; avoid fresh manure before planting.
Use fertile, firm soil. Lime acid ground if needed; tread firm and rake lightly. Collars or fine mesh guard against cabbage root fly.
Sowing & planting
Raise seedlings
Set and firm
Sow 

Use a nursery bed or modules. Space the seed thinly in rows or singly in cells. Cover and thin crowded seedlings before they become spindly. Sow Chinese cabbage where it will grow, or use modules to avoid disturbing its roots.

Transplant 

Harden off plants raised under cover. Lift nursery seedlings with soil around their roots. Set the lowest leaves at soil level, firm well and water. Use the final spacing for the type in Quick facts.

Looking after the crop
Keep mesh clear of leaves to exclude birds and caterpillars.
Hoe until plants suppress weeds. Keep soil firm; earth up stems loosened by wind or frost.
Water during drought. Use organic feed for weak plants as heads mature; avoid excess nitrogen before winter and soft, lush growth.
Remove yellow lower leaves, especially on winter cabbages and savoys, before they rot or shelter slugs.
Harvesting & storage
Thin spring rows for greens and leave room for the remaining plants to heart. Cut heads near ground level.
Cross-cut healthy spring or summer stumps for possible extra shoots. Remove diseased stumps; chop healthy stems for compost.
Lift sound winter heads before severe frost. Red and winter white types keep best. Strip loose leaves and store cool and dry on straw or in lined boxes. Check for rot.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Club root (finger and toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage caterpillars	Chewed leaves; caterpillars.	Pick off eggs and caterpillars; cover with fine mesh.
Cabbage root fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Fit collars or insect-proof mesh; rotate brassicas.
Pigeons	Leaves pecked or stripped.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Slugs and snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk. Clear yellow leaves near seedlings.
Flea beetle	Small holes; jumping beetles.	Mesh seedlings. Older plants tolerate small holes.
Mealy aphid	Grey colonies; curled leaves.	Tolerate minor colonies; squash damaging ones.
Final tips

Keep summer crops steadily watered.

Use spring thinnings as greens.

Check stored heads regularly for rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 106–111 · Growing Techniques 149–150
